Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Leila, a 53-year-old ship captain, sat in the consultation room with the quiet, watchful stillness of someone accustomed to reading the horizon for threats. She had come to therapy not because she believed it would help, but because her husband had finally insisted after she spent a third night pacing the living room, checking every lock twice, and then sitting in the dark by the front door until dawn. She had agreed, she said, to prove to him that nothing was wrong.

What was wrong began long before she ever set foot on a deck. When Leila was seven years old, living with her extended family in a tight-knit Middle Eastern community, her uncle—her mother’s brother, a man entrusted with her care while her parents worked—had beaten her regularly. The beatings were not impulsive; they were ritualized. He would call her into the back room, close the door, and tell her it was for her own good, that she had been disrespectful, that she needed to learn. She remembered the buckle of his belt most clearly, the way the light caught it before it fell. She remembered the sound it made against the thin cotton of her dress. But what she remembered most, and what she could not speak of without a strange hollow distance in her voice, was that after each beating, her mother would say nothing. Her father would look away. The community—the aunties, the neighbors, the imam—continued to praise her uncle as a devoted family man. No one intervened. No one asked. Leila learned early that the people who were supposed to protect her were not going to.

Now, decades later, Leila commanded a cargo vessel that sailed between Gulf ports and the Eastern Seaboard. She was respected, even feared, for her unflappable composure. But on the bridge, she found herself scanning radar and radio chatter with a vigilance that went far beyond professional duty. She listened for the wrong frequency, the wrong engine pitch, the wrong footstep behind her. She could not relax in her own cabin, even when the ship was at anchor in a calm harbor. She had come to believe that safety was an illusion, that danger was the baseline condition of existence, and that relaxing was simply an invitation for catastrophe. At night, she felt this most acutely. The dark amplified everything—the creak of the hull, the distant clang of a hatch, the sound of her own breathing. She had trained herself to sleep in short, shallow cycles, always half-awake, always listening for the sound of someone entering her space.

Her memories of the abuse came in fragments that did not obey any logic. Sometimes, without any warning, she would feel the full, crushing weight of terror—the helplessness, the shame, the burning sting across her back—but there would be no image attached to it. She would be standing at the helm, perfectly fine, and then suddenly she was seven years old again, her throat tight, her hands trembling, with no idea why. Other times, she could recall the event in precise detail, the buckle, the door closing, her uncle’s face, but she felt nothing at all. It was as if she were watching a stranger in a film, a girl who had nothing to do with her. She had come to think of that girl as someone she used to be, someone who was soft and trusting, someone who had believed that adults meant what they said. Leila had spent years trying not to think about her. She pushed the memories away, filled her mind with navigation charts, cargo manifests, engine diagnostics—anything concrete, anything she could control. But the harder she tried to suppress the past, the more it ambushed her in those wordless, imageless waves of feeling.

Her connection to her culture and community had eroded over time. She no longer attended community gatherings, avoided family weddings and funerals, and had stopped speaking Arabic with her children, though she had never explained why. She felt, in a way she could not articulate, that she had been exiled from something essential, that the people who should have held her safe had instead handed her over to harm. The world, she had concluded, was a dangerous place, and the only person she could trust was herself. That belief had made her an excellent captain. It had also made her profoundly alone.

What finally brought Leila to seek help was not the fear or the vigilance or the memories. It was the rumination. She found herself, during long night watches, replaying the beatings in her mind, trying to figure out what she could have done differently. If she had been quieter. If she had apologized faster. If she had told someone. She dwelled endlessly on the person she had been before—the trusting girl who laughed easily, who believed in fairness—and she grieved that girl as if she had died. She wanted her back. She was afraid she never would be.
